US consumer sentiment up on improved post-election utlook
article:
(Nov 20): US consumer sentiment picked up in November as gasoline prices fell, the outlook for business conditions improved and inflation expectations plunged.

The University of Michigan’s final sentiment index increased to 51.5 from 48 in October, according to the survey released Friday. The median estimate in a Bloomberg survey of economists projected November sentiment would rise to 51.6.

The university conducted its survey from Oct 20 through Nov 16, a span that saw Democrats take the House, the Senate and flip governorships in Georgia, Iowa, Texas, Ohio and Nevada during midterm elections.

The economy and affordability were key issues during the contest. Democrats’ sweeping victory in part reflected voter frustrations with high costs for food, gasoline, healthcare and housing.

Inflation expectations in the year ahead plummeted, the survey showed. Consumers expect prices to rise 3.7% over the next year, the lowest since February and down from 4.7% in October. They saw costs climbing at an annual rate of 3.3% over the next five to 10 years, also down from last month.

Consumer views of current conditions and expectations for the future both improved.

See also: Fed minutes show almost all officials expect more rate hikes

“Consumers appear to anticipate potential changes to public policy under a divided government to come,” Joanne Hsu, director of the survey, said in a statement. “Accordingly, the expectations index surged for independents.”

Following the election, expectations for gas prices sank and are now “broadly comparable to pre-Iran readings,” Hsu added.

A gauge of current personal finances also rose to the highest since July.

See also: US pending home sales fall to new record low on high rates

US households still face elevated inflation, with economists estimating that consumer prices rose about 4% from a year earlier in October. Borrowing costs are also high, with interest rates on a 30-year mortgage running above 7% since mid-September.

Relentless price increases helped push consumer sentiment to a record low in May and to the second-lowest level on record in October.

More recently, households have gotten some relief on at least one front: gasoline prices.

The national average price of a gallon of gasoline was above US$4 at the beginning of the month, according to data from AAA, but had dropped to about US$3.75 when the University of Michigan survey concluded.

title: Worldline sinks on Financial Times report on cash advances from customers
article:
(Nov 20): Worldline dropped as much as 20% after the Financial Times reported on the company’s internal actions in the years before 2023.

The French payments firm repeatedly delayed payments to suppliers and sought cash advances from customers ahead of results, the newspaper reported, citing documents and people familiar with the matter. Delaying payments and collecting customer money early is not illegal if contracts are not breached, the FT said in the report.

The stock was down about 15% at 1.16pm.

“Following the publication of a press article reporting allegations concerning the group’s past treasury practices and financial communication, Worldline wishes to reiterate that the company’s accounts are systematically reviewed by the audit committee, approved by the board of directors, certified by statutory auditors and approved by the shareholders,” it said in a statement. “They are produced in accordance with all applicable regulations and are free from any irregularities.”

Worldline also confirmed its outlook for 2026 “on a fully pruned basis”.

Its board “ensures that all serious concerns raised regarding the company are examined thoroughly and diligently, particularly within the framework of whistleblowing procedures,” according to the statement, which said that it “regrets the repetition of these past allegations”.

See also: Deutsche Bank probed by data watchdog as leak fallout spreads

It added that it’s “fully focused on implementing” its strategic plan, which has produced “results that are already tangible and encouraging.

Internal reports and messages show the firm restricted outflows and boosted inflows before half-yearly reporting dates from at least 2021 to 2023, the FT reported.

A PwC report prepared for Worldline in late 2023 estimated that the company’s reported free cash flow of €520 million in 2022 would have been €200 million lower without what it described as “optimisation” effects, according to the FT.

See also: France faces more strikes and protests over cost of living

The company has been struggling to win back investor confidence after allegations were made in newspaper reports last year that it had turned a blind eye to fraud. It announced the launch of a €392 million capital increase earlier this year as it sought to draw a line under the turmoil.
